processing: A drink, not a leaf style: black tea, often CTC, brewed without milk and finished with lime or lemon juice, sugar and a savoury spice mix such as black salt or jaljeera.
harvest_season: No harvest of its own, since it is made from everyday black tea all year round.
appearance_dry: Usually the small dark granules of ordinary CTC black tea.
appearance_liquor: Clear, thin reddish-amber, turned brighter and lighter by the citrus.
appearance_wet: Dark brown tea granules, normally strained away before serving.
taste_profile: Sour and sweet at once, with the sulphurous, salty edge of black salt over a brisk black tea base. Spice mixes vary, so one cup may be peppery and the next closer to digestive sweets.

brewing.notes: Brew strong, strain, then add sugar, a pinch of black salt or jaljeera, and the citrus last, off the heat, so it stays fresh. Season by taste.

vintage_note: Never sold by year or season: it is made to order from whatever black tea the stall or household keeps, typically inexpensive CTC. Fresh tea and fresh citrus matter far more than any vintage. Packet spice blends can stand in for the stallholder's own mix.
description:
Lebu cha is Bengal's lemon tea, and it is closer to a street snack in a cup than to a delicate infusion. Lebu means lemon or lime in Bengali, and the drink is black tea with citrus, sugar and something salty and spiced.

There is no fixed recipe. One published recipe combines lime, jaljeera, black salt, Hajmola and sugar; others use just lemon and rock salt, or pepper, ginger and palm sugar. The tea underneath is usually plain CTC, chosen because it stays strong through all of that.

Expect sour and sweet first, then the eggy, savoury note of black salt, and a brisk tea finish. The usual mistake is boiling the citrus with the tea, which dulls it, so add the juice at the end. Start with very little black salt, because a pinch too much takes over the cup.

There is nothing to look for on a packet, since it is not sold as a named tea. Use a robust, cheap black tea rather than a fine one, whose subtleties would disappear. Bengal's fragrant gondhoraj lime is a favoured choice where you can get it.
history: Little is documented about when or where lebu cha first appeared. It is associated with Kolkata, but no reliable account dates the drink or credits anyone with it, and the recipe seems to have spread by habit from stall to stall and home to home.
